target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove scheduling barriers for voters, especially low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably create paid time off or time away from work for private-sector employees, especially in retail, restaurants, caregiving, and other service jobs. Because many low-income workers would still be scheduled to work, a holiday could be mostly symbolic rather than actually improving access to voting.

target: AG1’s assumption that a national holiday by itself is the right solution to the scheduling problem.
objection: More direct alternatives are better, such as state laws requiring employer time off for voting and access reforms like expanded early voting, absentee/mail voting, automatic voter registration, and improved polling-site availability. These target the actual bottleneck more reliably than a calendar change.

target: AG1’s broader premise that an election-day holiday is a dependable way to increase turnout.
objection: Research and election-management experience suggest that an election-day holiday by itself is not a reliable turnout-boosting strategy compared with other voting access reforms.

target: AG1’s idea that the holiday could be designed to ensure people have time to vote.
objection: If the policy must include enforceable employer time-off rules to work, then the useful part is the time-off mandate itself, not the holiday label. In that case, calling it a national holiday is redundant or distracting rather than essential.

target: AG1’s claim that holidays solve the problem of voter scheduling for workers.
objection: A holiday does not automatically change the schedules of essential and shift workers in retail, food service, caregiving, and similar jobs, so many low-income workers still face the same practical conflict between work and voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday will reduce Election Day congestion or wait-time problems.
objection: A national holiday could concentrate voting into a single day and create longer lines and reduced capacity at polling places if staffing and polling-site resources do not scale up, shifting the barrier from work schedules to waiting times.

target: AG1’s idea that a holiday is a useful structural fix for Election Day access.
objection: A federal holiday is a blunt, one-size-fits-all tool: it may benefit workers whose employers already observe the day while still leaving the most disadvantaged workers without guaranteed paid or protected time. More targeted reforms that spread voting over time are better for access quality.

target: AG1’s argument that a national holiday is valuable because it is a uniform federal change.
objection: Uniformity alone does not solve the real bottleneck unless employers are compelled to provide usable time off. If private employers stay open and do not grant paid or protected time, low-income workers still face the same scheduling constraint.

target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a holiday reduces reliance on individual requests for time off.
objection: Even if schedules become somewhat more predictable, workers can still face employer discretion, skeleton staffing, unpaid leave, or the need to request accommodations from managers. A holiday does not remove that gatekeeping.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday helps election capacity by increasing poll workers and easing logistics.
objection: Election capacity can be improved directly through funding for poll workers, training, overtime pay, and expanded polling locations without changing the employment calendar. A holiday can also concentrate demand into one day and worsen the capacity problem.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday makes it easier for workers to get to polling places by reducing routine and transportation barriers.
objection: Transportation convenience does not solve the main issue for low-income shift workers, which is having time away from the job during polling hours. States and localities can instead use extended polling hours, more polling places, mobile sites, and transportation support without relying on a holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday makes voting simpler and lowers procedural friction.
objection: A holiday does not remove registration cutoffs, ID/document requirements, ballot-request steps, or confusion about polling locations. Those administrative barriers still require access reforms such as automatic voter registration and other procedural simplifications.

target: AG1’s concern that broader voting-access reforms could crowd out or reduce urgency for change.
objection: Making Election Day a national holiday could become a political substitute that reduces lawmakers’ incentive to enact and enforce stronger, mechanism-specific reforms like paid/protected time off and access expansions.

target: AG1’s claim that bundling a holiday with time-to-vote and access reforms makes the holiday worthwhile.
objection: If enforceable workplace time-to-vote rules and access reforms are already in the package, the holiday status itself is mostly redundant. The real work is being done by the enforceable protections and access changes, not the holiday label.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday makes it easier for workers to use time-to-vote rights without negotiating with managers.
objection: A holiday does not automatically create usable time in the workplaces where low-income people work, because employers can stay open and keep staffing. Without direct, enforceable time-to-vote requirements, workers still may have to choose between work and voting.

target: AG1’s argument that a national holiday creates a civic norm that increases participation.
objection: Even if a holiday makes voting feel more important, that does not help low-income hourly workers who are still constrained by work schedules. The civic-norm effect does not solve the access problem without employer-neutral, enforceable time off.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday makes time off feel more legitimate and therefore easier for workers to use.
objection: A holiday does not eliminate enforcement problems or ensure employers honor paid/protected time without retaliation. The decisive factor is still clear, enforceable rights with penalties for noncompliance, so the holiday is not enough on its own.
